full_judgment:
2. Shorn of unnecessary details, the fact of the case lies in a very short compus. The petitioner as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 441 of 2012 in the court of Joint District Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka, on the following prayers: 

 "(a) A decree of declaration that the Sales Contract No. S 00831 dated 30-10-2010 and Sales Contract No. S 00955 dated 3-12-2010 are illegal, void, inoperative and having no binding effect upon the plaintiff and the Arbitration Clauses contained therein is unenforceable; 

 (b) a decree of declaration that the reciprocal performance under Sales Contract No. S 00831 dated 30-10-2010 and Sales Contract No. S 00955 dated 3-12-2010 having become void, the plaintiff is discharged from all liabilities in respect of or arising out of the said Sales Contract No. S00831 dated 30-10-2010 and Sales Contract No. S 00955 dated 3-12-2010; 

 the defendant No. 1 carries on business in Bangladesh through its agent, the defendant No. 2. The plaintiff in the course of its business approached the defendant No. 2 for supplying certain quantity of raw cotton from the defendant No. 1. The defendant No. 2 representing defendant No. 1 arranged two contracts to be executed between the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1, namely Sales Contract: S 00831 dated 30-10-2010 and Sales Contract: S 00955 dated 3-12-2010 for sale of about 500 metric ton (MT) of BURKINA FASO RAW COTTON and for 1000 metric ton (MT) respectively. 

 In these circumstances, the plaintiff requested the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 to revise the price since the market price of raw cotton had become substantially lower than the contract prices. But the defendant No. 2 instead of giving favourable response forwarded two back dated pro forma invoices both dated 18-2-2011 to the plaintiff in respect of the said contracts. However, since performance of the said contacts are required by opening of L/C the plaintiff approached the officials of the pro forma defendant No. 8, bank for opening L/C. But it was informed to the plaintiff by the pro forma defendant No. 8 that the proposed L/Cs may not be opened because of the Regulations and Circulars issued by the pro forma defendant No. 9 (Bangladesh Bank), which prohibits banks from opening of L/C at a price which is excessively higher than the market price and thus opening of L/C at a much higher price may give rise to an issue of money laundering. Despite the situation aforesaid, since performance of the said contracts are required by opening L/C and since the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 refused to reduce the contract prices to bring it in line with the prevailing market price, the plaintiff by its letter No. PHP/SP/APR/2011 dated 10-4-2011 made an application to the pro forma defendant No. 8 to open L/C for importing the contracted cotton. But the bank replied to the plaintiff declining to open L/C at a price higher than the market price prevalent on the date of opening L/C. 

 4. Since the price of the cotton was not competitive at the time of opening L/C, pro forma defendant No. 8 refused to open the L/C on the plea that it would violate the provisions of the Import Policy Order 2009-2012 and the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947, thus the contract is unlawful and void under section 23 of the Contract Act, 1872. For the aforesaid reasons the plaintiff was unable to open L/C and the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 had been regularly made aware of the above developments in various ways. 

 5. The defendant No. 1 by its letter dated 3-2-2012 alleged that the plaintiff was in breach of the said contracts due to its failure to open L/C and also stated that the market value of the cotton had fallen to 100.21 USC/LB and threatened the plaintiff that unless it opens L/C, it would initiate arbitration proceedings with the defendant No. 3 i.e. International Cotton Association Limited ("ICA") claiming the market difference of US$ 4,581,930.41 on 1500 MT plus total carrying charges of US$ 1,065,924.10. In the situations aforesaid, the petitioner company has become constrained to file the suit against the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 for declaration and injunction. 

 6. At the time of filing of the suit the plaintiff filed an application under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure ("CPC") praying for temporary injunction to restrain the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1-2 from pursuing any claim whatsoever relating to the sales contract S 00839 dated 30-10-2010 and sales contract S 00955 dated 3-12-2010 before the International Cotton Association Limited ("ICA"), Liverpool, United Kingdom or elsewhere and also to restrain defendant-opposite party Nos. 3-7 from proceeding further with Arbitration No. ICA reference: A01/2012/31 and from passing any award thereon till disposal of the suit and also prayed for an order of ad interim injunction in line with the prayer for temporary injunction till hearing of the application for temporary injunction. 

 7. The learned Joint District Judge, 4th court, Dhaka, after hearing by its order dated 13-5-2012 did not consider the plaintiff's prayer for ad interim injunction even did not consider to issue any notice to show cause upon the defendants rather fixed the matter for hearing on 13-7-2012 without assigning any reason whatsoever which amounts to rejection of the prayer for injunction. 

 9. The opposite party No. 1 contested the Rule by filing counter affidavit and supplementary affidavit to the counter affidavit denying the claim of the plaintiff contending inter alia, that the opposite party No. 1 is a company incorporated under the relevant law of Switzerland and carrying on business of procuring cotton from different country of the world and supplying the same to the purchasers. 

 11. The plaintiff-petitioner with a malafide intention did not open L/C in due time even after repeated reminders sent by the defendant-opposite party No.1, thus the petitioner was in breach of the contract. The plaintiff-petitioner knowing fully well about the arbitration clause in the contract and despite clear knowledge deliberately cause delay by writing various letters to the defendant No. 1 to reduce the price of cotton using unfair tactics. The defendant-opposite party No.1 in clear term by several letter refused to reduce the price of the cotton. Due to continuous non-cooperation by the plaintiff-petitioner, the defendant-opposite party No. 1 finding no other way out invoked the arbitration clause of the contract and sent a request for arbitration on 8-2-2012 to the ICA. By a letter dated 9-2-2012; the ICA informed the plaintiff-petitioner that they have received a request for arbitration from defendant-opposite party No. 1 and also informed that the opposite party No.1 had already nominated their arbitrator and the petitioner was advised to appoint their arbitrator within 14 days of the receipt of the letter. 

 12. But the petitioner failed to do needful in this regard. Thereafter, it was informed to the plaintiff-petitioner by a letter dated 28-2-2012 that it had failed to nominate an arbitrator within the stipulated time. Resultantly, ICA nominated its president an arbitrator on behalf of the plaintiff-petitioner and it was duly notified to them. The arbitration manager by letter dated 22-1-2012 informed the plaintiff-petitioner regarding appointment of the Chairman of the Arbitration Tribunal with a copy of the same. But the plaintiff-petitioner did not participate in the arbitration proceeding rather remain silent about their participation in the proceedings. The arbitration manager by different letters communicated about arbitration proceedings to the plaintiff-petitioner and its progress thereof. The petitioner instead of appearing before the arbitration tribunal as per terms and conditions of the contract filed title suit along with an application for injunction before the Joint District Judge 4th court, Dhaka, who after hearing the application kept the same for further hearing fixing 13-7-2012. Being failed in their attempt the plaintiff-petitioner moved this Court by filing this revisional application and obtained the present Rule and order of ad interim injunction. 

 13. Mr Ramzan Ali Sikder, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner at the very outset submits that when an application seeking injunction is filed before any court, the court is to consider the application giving top most priority of the same and it is the obligation of the court to dispose of the application either allowing or rejecting the same. But, in the instant suit though the plaintiff moved an application for temporary injunction and prayed for an ad interim injunction till disposal of the substantive application the trial court did not pass any order either granting an ad interim order of injunction or issuing notice to show cause to the defendants which amounts to rejection of the application filed by the plaintiff-petitioner. He further submits that the plaintiff-petitioner could not materialize the contract and open letter of credit through bank in Bangladesh because of an embargo imposed by the Bangladesh Bank to the effect that the bank in Bangladesh cannot be allowed to open L/C for import of any good from foreign country at a higher price than the price prevalent in the market at the relevant time. Mr Sikder also argued that the contract provides price of the cotton much higher than the prices prevalent in the world market as such, the concern bank of the plaintiff-petitioner refused to open letter of credit for importation of the good under contract which was absolutely beyond the control of the plaintiff-petitioner and for such an embargo the contract itself came to an end because of the law of the land. 

 14. He further goes to argue that the contract could not be executed not because of the lathes or negligence of the plaintiff-petitioner but it is for the law of the land, as such, the plaintiff-petitioner cannot be held liable for non-performance of the contract and the plaintiff-petitioner is not at all liable to pay any differences in price of the cotton as well as carrying charges to the supplier. But the defendant-opposite party No. 1 basing on a defunct contract initiated an arbitration proceeding claiming a huge amount from the plaintiff-petitioner for which Title Suit No. 441 of 2012 has been filed seeking declaration and injunction against the action of the opposite party No. 1 and in the suit the plaintiff sought an order of ad interim injunction, but the court below without considering urgency of the matter most unfortunately instead of granting injunction and issuing notice to show cause to the opposite party fixed the matter for hearing after two months fixing 13-7-2012 and, as such, the trial court has committed an error of law in the decision occasioning failure of justice for which the plaintiff-petitioner moved this Court and obtained the instant Rule along with an order of ad interim injunction. 

 15. Mr Junayed Ahmed Chowdhury, learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No.1 submits that, admittedly the plaintiff-petitioner entered into two sale contacts with defendant-opposite party No. 1 for purchase of 1500 MT cotton. As per, terms and condition of the contract the plaintiff-petitioner was under an obligation to open the L/C in accordance with the terms of the contract which went unheeded by the plaintiff-petitioner. He further submits that the defendant-opposite party No. 1 by its letter dated 3-2-2012 reminded the petitioner that by its failure to do so the plaintiff-petitioner was in breach of the contract and reminded about arbitration clause but the petitioner paid no heed to the repeated reminders of the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 and refrained themselves from opening L/C in time as per, terms of the contract. Resultantly, the opposite party No. 1 under the terms and condition of the contract requested ICA for arbitration with due notification to the plaintiff-petitioner. The ICA once again requested the plaintiff-petitioner to nominate their arbitrator, but the petitioner miserably failed to appoint their arbitrator and to make response to the letters written to them by ICA regarding appointment of Chairman of the Arbitration Tribunal and progress and time to time development of the arbitration proceedings. The petitioner's non co-operation in resolving the dispute by arbitration, the Arbitration  Tribunal proceeded with the arbitration as per law and finally passed an award resolving the dispute between the parties. Meanwhile, the petitioner instead of taking part in the arbitration proceedings moved before the Joint District Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka, by filing Title Suit No. 441 of 2012 wherein prayed for an order of injunction but failed and subsequently obtained this instant Rule and order of ad interim injunction. 

 16. Mr Chowdhury further submits that the opposite party being a foreign company the order of ad interim injunction passed by this Court though served upon the opposite party No. 1, but the injunction order does not extend because the opposite party resides outside the territory of Bangladesh. It is also argued that, the opposite party No. I appeared before the trial court on 5-8-2012 and, as such, there was no violation of the order of injunction by the opposite party No. 1. Mr Chowdhury further submits that the petitioner being a party to the contract their remedy lies under the terms and conditions of contract in particular by arbitration as contained in the contract entered in between the parties, but the petitioner by passing the terms of the contract moved before the court in Bangladesh seeking injunction to restrain the Arbitration Tribunal functioning beyond the territory of Bangladesh. As such, by any order of Bangladeshi court who is residing outside Bangladesh and a proceeding initiated therein cannot be restrained. He further submits that meanwhile, the arbitration proceedings ended with pronouncement of an award as such, the prayer as made by the petitioner for restraining the opposite party from doing certain act have became over. Therefore, application for injunction filed by the plaintiff-petitioner in its present from not at all maintainable as the court can restrain any person or authority from doing any act in future not an act already done. However, the plaintiff-petitioner may agitate their grievance before the trial court by getting the title suit heard and disposed of, if there be any, not by filing any application or seeking injunction in the form now they are praying. Finally, he argued that the prayer as made in the title suit by the plaintiff-petitioner has also become infructuous, because of pronouncement of the award by the Arbitration Tribunal. Referring to the prayers made to the plaint in suit, Mr Chowdhury further submits that all the prayers contained in the plaint in Title Suit No. 441 of 2012 cannot be given by the court, where the subject matter is not in existence. As such, not only the prayer for injunction but also the suit as a whole is not maintainable, hence, the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

 18. The plaintiff-petitioner filed the title suit praying for two declarations and for a decree of permanent injunction along with ad interim injunction restraining the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 from purusing any claim whatsoever relating to the sale contacts in question before the International Cotton Association Limited or elsewhere and the defendant-opposite party Nos. 3-7 from proceeding further with the Arbitration No. ICA reference: A01/2012/31 and from passing any award thereon. 

 19. The trial court by the impugned order dated 13-5-2012 kept the application for hearing on 13-7-2012 without issuing any show cause and passing any order as prayed for. Generally, considering urgency of the matter the court is to hear and dispose of the same giving top most priority but in the instant case it appears that on the very day of filing suit an application for temporary injunction moved before the trial court the trial court was under an obligation in law either to issue notice to show cause to the opposite party or issuing show cause to pass an order of ad interim injunction as prayed for. In the alternative if the trial court finds no prima facie case in favour of the applicant it may reject the application summarily without granting any injunction or issuing any notice to show cause to other party. But from impugned order this Court finds that the trial court recorded no reason for fixing the matter for hearing after two months of filing of the application for injunction which caused serious injustice to the party who came before the court with an application for injunction. In not issuing any notice to show cause or granting any order of injunction or rejecting the application for injunction stating reason the trial court has committed serious error of law occasioning failure of justice. 

 21. Order of this Court was communicated to the Arbitration Tribunal on 28-5-2012 by a letter from the lawyer of the plaintiff-petitioner. After communication of the order the Arbitration Tribunal proceeded with the arbitration proceeding and passed award on 13-7-2012. Apparently the said award was passed during subsistence of the order of injunction. The petitioner claims that the said award passed during pendency of the Rule as well as the suit in violation of the order of the court and, as such, the award is a nullity. On the other hand the opposite-party claim that the order passed by this Court restraining arbitration tribunal resides in another country beyond the territorial jurisdiction of this Court and, as such, under no circumstances any person or authority of another country can be restrained by an order of this Court from doing any act. Therefore, the Arbitration Tribunal was not bound to obey or refrain from proceeding with the arbitration proceedings and there was no violation of any order as claimed by the petitioner. 

 23. In the instant Rule the petitioner prayed for restraining the opposite party from proceeding with the arbitration proceeding, but the proceeding is now not in existence. In this precarious situation the opposite party claims that the relief for the petitioner-plaintiff is to challenge the award under the provision as contained in Arbitration Act, not by filing any suit or seeking any restrain order in the form they prayed for. It appears that the plaintiff has filed the suit on the ground that the agreement entered in between the parties have become inoperative, void and not binding effect upon the plaintiff and also for a decree of permanent injunction from pursuing any claim whatsoever relating to any contract in question and upon such prayer the plaintiff is required to show its prima facie case before the trial court to get an order of injunction. 

 24. From the argument as made by the learned Advocates for the parties it appears that the plaintiff in order to obtain an order of ad interim injunction relied upon their prima facie case in the suit that the contract itself became frustrated and the defendant relied upon the various provisions contained in Arbitration Act and the case Manzoor Hussain vs Wali Mohammad reported in 17 DLR (SC) 369 in which at paragraph 28 it has been held that: 

 "the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act does not forbid the making of a contract which may contemplate doing a thing which is contrary to the provisions of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, for, that thing can still be done by ex post facto permission of the State Bank of Pakistan. The scheme of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, therefore, is not to forbid the making of a contract but merely to insist that the contract shall be performed in a particular manner, namely, by taking the necessary permission of the competent authority. It cannot, therefore, in the circumstances, be said that a contract which violates any of the terms of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act is ex facie or ab initio void or comes within the mischief of a contract prohibited by section 23 of the contract Act." 

 26. The trial court having not passed any order on the application for temporary injunction filed by the plaintiff-petitioner, this Court, therefore, decided to dispose of the Rule without entering into the merit of the suit giving a direction to the trial court to dispose of the application filed by the plaintiff-petitioner giving an opportunity to the defendant-opposite parties to file written objection within a shortest possible time preferably within one month from the date of receipt of this judgment. However, in that case the plaintiff be given an opportunity to take appropriate step for seeking further relief and making alternative prayer as to injunction if so advised.
